director.chapterArc: Domestic alarm and lost time narrow into a deliberate risk calculation; the crossing becomes controlled tactical defense, then an accelerating trap. The fallen mule and lost hook fracture that control. Callie’s desperate return becomes an impossible impact, followed by dissociated, effortless violence and a final stillness in which neither she nor Katori can name what has happened.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder grounded, measured, and physically precise. Let fear register through arithmetic, breath, weight, and spatial consequence—not generalized urgency. The supernatural change is an impersonal bodily fact, never a triumphant spectacle. After every temporary color, restore Calder’s usual warmth, pitch center, accent, cadence, and emotional distance completely.

cues.delivery: Land the understatement with exhausted maternal dryness; the humor acknowledges the alarming fact without diminishing it.
cues.from: Her mother looked at the sky for a while. "Well," she said. "That's new."
cues.through: Her mother looked at the sky for a while. "Well," she said. "That's new."
cues.reason: A brief pressure release reveals the mother’s sharpness before the practical consequences resume.

cues.delivery: Make the dry mouth and arithmetic carry the dread. Callie forces each cost into the open, keeping her voice useful rather than frightened.
cues.from: Callie's mouth was very dry.
cues.through: "The causeway," she said. "There's no turning on it. If it's bad in the middle we go forward or we go nowhere, and I want that said before anybody agrees with me."
cues.reason: The crossing becomes a conscious commitment with no retreat.

cues.delivery: Let Pell’s solidarity remain hidden inside bookkeeping and logistics; firm, unsentimental protection with no softening of his authority.
cues.from: Pell already had the pencil out. He wrote for a moment, and then turned the book around so Callie could see it, and there in the small neat hand at the bottom of the day's page was: Causeway at dusk. C.'s call. Concur — K., P.
cues.through: C.'s call.
cues.reason: The group deliberately shares responsibility for Callie’s decision.

cues.delivery: Read the three-word ledger notation plainly and precisely as written initials, with no emotional coloring or flourish.
cues.from: Concur — K., P.
cues.through: Concur — K., P.
cues.reason: Three targeted care-colored Fish pickups stayed far below the naturalness floor on this terse written notation; a neutral base-narrator take preserves Pell's bookkeeping restraint and isolates the letters cleanly.

cues.delivery: Let Pell’s solidarity remain hidden inside bookkeeping and logistics; firm, unsentimental protection with no softening of his authority.
cues.from: "That's not to blame you with," Pell said.
cues.through: "That's not to blame you with," Pell said. "That's so that in a year when somebody says it was a fool's decision I can show them the three of us made it together and what we knew when we made it." He put the pencil behind his ear. "Get up on the wagon and don't walk the first half mile. I want you fresh at the far end, not the near one."
cues.reason: The group deliberately shares responsibility for Callie’s decision.

cues.delivery: Mark the instant spare time disappears. Keep the multiplying bodies spatially clear, while Callie’s unnaturally steady report contains the first surge of panic.
cues.from: And that was the last decision anybody got to make with time to spare in it.
cues.through: "Mass on the west," she said. Her voice came out much steadier than she was. "West is the mass. East is three, four — east is small."
cues.reason: The encounter reverses from manageable contact into a mass attack.

cues.delivery: Project the tactical correction forward over the noise; urgent and intelligible, never shrill.
cues.from: "Don't kill them," she shouted forward. "Tip them — don't kill them —"
cues.through: "Don't kill them," she shouted forward. "Tip them — don't kill them —"
cues.reason: Callie genuinely shouts a crucial instruction that the others cannot hear.

cues.delivery: Let understanding arrive first in the body, then become a cold chain of facts. Stress the closed logic of the trap, not supernatural menace.
cues.from: She was magnificent and she was making it worse with every single one, and Callie understood that a full four seconds before she understood why, in the way you sometimes solve a thing with your stomach before your head catches up.
cues.through: That was the trap and there was no way out through the front of it.
cues.reason: Callie realizes their most effective defense is attracting and multiplying the threat.

cues.delivery: A full warning torn out by necessity; strike the command cleanly and release it immediately.
cues.from: "Katori!" she screamed. "Stop putting it down!"
cues.through: "Katori!" she screamed. "Stop putting it down!"
cues.reason: The manuscript explicitly gives Callie a scream at the crisis point.

cues.delivery: Otto’s bellow is a functional demand for missing counts, broad enough to cross the battle noise but still disciplined.
cues.from: "Where's four and five?" Otto bellowed.
cues.through: "Where's four and five?" Otto bellowed.
cues.reason: A genuine shouted question briefly cuts through the action.

cues.delivery: Deliver the answer bone-dry and occupied, as professional pride rather than a joke offered for relief.
cues.from: "I've been making them count for eleven years."
cues.through: "I've been making them count for eleven years."
cues.reason: Ines’s compressed retort supplies earned dark humor without relaxing the danger.

cues.delivery: Give Pell’s broken shout and the unseen fall blunt physical shock. Keep the mule’s death unexamined, then make the widening gap and horse panic brutally legible.
cues.from: Callie did not see how. She heard Pell shouting — a high, cracked, appalling sound out of a man who had not raised his voice once in nine days — and she turned in time to watch the whole wagon lurch a foot and a half sideways as the traces went slack on one side, and then the mule was simply not there, and there was a noise from down on the rock that she put away somewhere and did not take out again for a long time.
cues.through: And on the near side of the pole, still harnessed, still buckled into a trace that now ran twenty feet down a slope of broken rock to a weight that was not going to move again, the horse went out of her mind.
cues.reason: The wagon’s defensive geometry collapses and the team loses control of the horse.

cues.delivery: Treat the descent as compulsion rather than bravery. Count the exposed movements clearly and let the stupidity of the choice remain coldly apparent.
cues.from: Callie stood on the shoulder of the causeway and looked down twenty feet of broken rock at her grandfather's hook, wedged between two slabs with a dead grey shape coming apart around it, and there was no part of the decision in her at all.
cues.through: It took eleven seconds and it was the stupidest thing she had ever done. She went down on three points the way they did, and got her boot wedged, and got it back, and reached the hook and hauled it out of the slabs with both hands and a noise she did not hear herself make.
cues.reason: Callie abandons safety to retrieve the irreplaceable hook.

cues.delivery: Hush the passage around the mother’s spent voice. Her use of Callie’s name carries recognition and surrender, not melodramatic farewell.
cues.from: Not screamed it. Said it. The wagon bed was above and behind her, up past the lip of the embankment, out of her sight entirely, and across all of that noise, in a voice that had no strength left in it to be loud with, her mother said, "Callie," in the tone of somebody who has just seen the shape of the next four seconds and is letting go of them.
cues.through: Not screamed it. Said it. The wagon bed was above and behind her, up past the lip of the embankment, out of her sight entirely, and across all of that noise, in a voice that had no strength left in it to be loud with, her mother said, "Callie," in the tone of somebody who has just seen the shape of the next four seconds and is letting go of them.
cues.reason: The mother quietly foresees the immediate danger and has no strength to shout.

cues.delivery: Build through exact distances and competing threats. Keep Callie’s run clear and purposeful; at the raised hoof, narrow into a child’s involuntary defense rather than heroic action.
cues.from: Two of them were over the tailgate. They had come up the rear of the embankment while the whole world was looking at the gap, and they were on the bed, in among the crates, three feet from where her mother lay with her back against the boards.
cues.through: And Callie did the oldest thing there is. She did not duck and she did not step and she did not do one single one of the things eleven years of her grandfather's teaching had put into her body. She threw her arms up in front of her face, the way a child does, the way anybody does, and she shut her eyes.
cues.reason: Callie races toward her mother while failing to register the horse’s lethal movement.

cues.delivery: Slow into impersonal scale. The force is ancient, weight-bearing, and already present—not benevolent, radiant, or theatrical.
cues.from: Something closed over her.
cues.through: Something took the other side of the yoke and pulled with her.
cues.reason: Callie first encounters the hidden power beneath her ordinary bodily effort.

cues.delivery: Give the hoof impact enormous weight, then make the absence of transmitted force unnervingly exact. Preserve the rebound’s physics; do not celebrate it.
cues.from: The hoof hit.
cues.through: The horse came off it. Four hundred kilos of animal at the end of a full kick rebounded off a thirteen-year-old girl standing in a road, and staggered sideways into the pole with her hindquarters, and screamed.
cues.reason: The expected injury is replaced by impossible immunity and violent recoil.

cues.delivery: Use estranged, matter-of-fact wonder. The shield feels wearable and inescapable; the hook’s extension is wrong, cold, and unchosen—not a heroic weapon reveal.
cues.from: It was on her. That was the only word she had and it was not the right one. It was closed over her from her boots to the crown of her head, a skin's thickness off her everywhere at once, and she could feel it the way you feel a coat — not as a thing out in front of her, but as a thing she was wearing — and she understood, with a clarity that had no explanation anywhere behind it, that she could not get it off.
cues.through: It was not a sword. Callie had seen a sword twice in her life and it was not one. She had not chosen a single thing about it.
cues.reason: Callie recognizes two simultaneous bodily and material transformations.

cues.delivery: Observe the ash parting with quiet precision, then let forbidden certainty settle without explanation or triumph.
cues.from: She could see perfectly well through it. She had walked eleven paces in it and it had come with her, every step, the way a coat comes with you. The ash running down the camber of the road reached her boots and did not touch them. It parted, and went around her, and closed up again on the downhill side, and left her standing in a clean dry shape of road exactly the size of a girl.
cues.through: She was holding both of them. At the same time. She could feel the weight of each one separately, and she knew — without one single person ever having told her anything about any of it — that she was not supposed to be able to.
cues.reason: The clean outline around Callie proves the shield persists, and she knows the dual manifestation should be impossible.

cues.delivery: Let Callie’s voice fracture small rather than loud. The unfinished sentence is loss of vocabulary and control; the final question seeks a rule that might contain her.
cues.from: "Katori." Callie's voice came apart on her. "I can't put it down. Either of them. I can't — "
cues.through: "Which one is it?" she said.
cues.reason: Her competence collapses into a hushed plea for an explanation Katori cannot provide.
